extracted.intended_audience: European patent practitioners (patent attorneys, examiners, appellants) and others working on EPC inventive-step analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on applying the EPO 'problem and solution' approach to assess inventive step under Article 56 EPC, focusing on correct formulation of the objective technical problem, choice of starting point, combination of prior art, and treatment of non-technical features. Intended to help practitioners and examiners avoid ex post facto reasoning and ensure consistency with the statutory test of Article 56.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of inventive step (Article 56 EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: "An invention shall be considered as involving an inventive step if, having regard to the state of the art, it is not obvious to a person skilled in the art."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the sole statutory definition of inventive step — the assessment must be whether the invention is obvious having regard to the state of the art. The problem-and-solution approach is only a tool and must be applied consistently with this definition; it cannot displace the Article 56 test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the state of the art (Article 54(2) EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The state of the art shall be held to comprise everything made available to the public by means of a written or oral description, by use, or in any other way, before the date of filing of the European patent application."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All public disclosures before the relevant date are relevant. Obviousness must be assessed with regard to this whole body of prior art, not limited to particular documents unless chosen for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-and-solution approach is a tool, not a definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem-and-solution approach is widely used by the EPO as a method of analysis but is not the definition of inventive step in the EPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the approach only insofar as it is compatible with Article 56; ensure the steps and formulations used in the approach reflect what is obvious from the state of the art rather than introducing extraneous material or ex post facto pointers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each link in the chain (state of the art → problem → solution) must be obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument that a claimed invention lacks inventive step via the problem-and-solution chain is only valid if every stage is obvious; if any stage is not obvious, lack of inventive step is not established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing lack of inventive step, demonstrate both (a) that the problem is known or obvious from the state of the art and (b) that the solution is obvious in view of the state of the art. If the path relies on information beyond the state of the art, the reasoning fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem must be known or obvious in view of the state of the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The formulation of the (objective technical) problem used in the problem-and-solution analysis must itself be obvious or known having regard to the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the chosen problem is not obvious from the state of the art, the problem-and-solution analysis is invalid and the problem should be reformulated (often to a less ambitious, obvious problem such as 'can I improve this?'). Avoid formulating the problem so it contains or points to the claimed solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem must not contain pointers to the technical solution (avoid ex post facto formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective technical problem must be formulated so as not to contain pointers to the technical solution; including part of the technical solution in the problem leads to ex post facto reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Board of Appeal guidance (e.g., G-VII,5.2; T 229/85; T 800/91): formulate a problem the skilled person would recognize from the prior art alone. Do not derive the problem by taking undue account of the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulation of the problem must not itself be inventive ('problem invention')
rubrics_metrics.description: If the formulation of the problem is itself inventive, then an otherwise obvious solution to that problem can amount to an invention — the problem formulation cannot be the source of inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and reject 'problem inventions' (see T 0002/83). If the problem identification requires inventive activity, the problem-and-solution route to show lack of inventive step is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem may be obvious in view of the state of the art as a whole (combining prior art disclosures)
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem need only be obvious having regard to the state of the art as a whole, not necessarily evident from the chosen starting document alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is permissible to draw the problem (and the solution) from different prior art documents, but care must be taken to ensure the combination is itself obvious and that the disclosures are contextually compatible. Demonstrate why a skilled person would combine the disclosures and that nothing makes the combination non-obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care when combining distinct prior art disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: When the problem and solution are made obvious by different documents (e.g., D1 shows the starting arrangement, D2 indicates the problem, D3 discloses a solution), it is necessary to ensure the combination of D2 and D3 (directly or indirectly) would be obvious to the skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check contextual applicability (e.g., D2 may indicate a problem only in a particular context incompatible with D3), and explain why the skilled person would have had a reason to combine the teachings. Avoid unjustified cross-context combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of starting point (closest prior art) — any appropriate starting point may be used
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 56 requires non-obviousness having regard to the state of the art, not in relation to a single 'closest' prior art; any prior art item that yields an obvious path to the claimed invention suffices as a starting point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no single 'wrong' starting point: if an obvious path from any piece of prior art to the claim can be shown, the claim lacks inventive step. It is often unnecessary to spend excessive effort to identify the unique closest prior art; examine several promising starting points as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of non-technical features (Comvik approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Comvik approach, inventive step can only be provided by technical features (or by non-technical features that in combination with technical features produce a technical effect). Non-technical features that do not contribute to a technical effect cannot be regarded as part of the solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include novel non-technical features as part of the problem unless they are known/obvious from the state of the art; the practice of treating non-technical features as mere constraints on the problem (when they are novel) appears incompatible with the requirement that the problem be known/obvious. Review and apply relevant case law (Comvik T 0641/00 and subsequent decisions) carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure requirement in Rule 42 EPC (description must disclose technical problem and solution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 42(1)(c) EPC: the description shall disclose the invention, as claimed, in such terms that the technical problem, even if not expressly stated as such, and its solution can be understood, and state any advantageous effects of the invention with reference to the background art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a disclosure/description requirement (ensuring the application explains the technical problem and solution) and not a definition of inventive step. Ensure applications disclose the problem and advantageous effects relative to the prior art, but remember this does not replace the Article 56 obviousness test.
